text:
Recent evidence supports attribute composition, but provides limited direct validation for a title/description encoder learned entirely from scratch inside BERT4Rec. [MARS (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.00702) learns multiple attribute-aware representations and attribute-wise matching, motivating finer distinctions than one global semantic vector. However, it uses pretrained language models and structured attributes including brand/category; its gains do not establish effectiveness with only supplied titles/descriptions. [DenseRec (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.18442) reports that semantic similarity can miss differences in user appeal and contextual relevance. Its cold-start improvements mainly concern sequence representations containing unseen items; experiments use pretrained content embeddings and SASRec, so transfer to this constrained BERT4Rec setup remains a hypothesis.

A reasonable experiment is a small shared token encoder, randomly initialized and jointly optimized with BERT4Rec’s masked-item objective, composing title/description features with item-ID embeddings within one network. Shared tokens could transfer interaction supervision to sparse items, but rare model numbers, negation and compatibility phrases may remain poorly learned. Treat explicit missing-text handling, token dropout and title-versus-description ablations as proposed safeguards, not established findings. Check validation performance by item frequency and text availability to detect shortcuts from repeated wording or brand-like tokens. Crucially, metadata similarity and purchase sequences do not establish physical compatibility, purpose or fulfilled demand: [exposure/satisfaction research (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ins.2024.120834) highlights that observed interactions can reflect exposure and promotion rather than satisfaction. Preserve the single BERT4Rec model and infer no unavailable attributes.
